newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Zeitler - no reason for German rate rise soon.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Zeitler - no reason for German rate rise soon.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler said on Tuesday that he saw no reason for an upturn in German interest rates in the foreseeable future but added that this did not rule out the possibility of temporary corrections on the capital market.

Zeitler also said he saw no danger of an increase in German inflation at present because economic growth was modest, wage deals had been moderate and raw materials prices were having a dampening impact.

But he added that the import of price stability through the mark's strength in recent years was now over. Import prices had risen at an annualised rate of 6.5 percent compared with the end of August last year, Zeitler said.

"The (Bundesbank's) central council used the scope for interest rate cuts last year and did not allow itself to be impressed by 'historical levels'," Zeitler said, referring to the reduction in the main money market rate, or repo, to an all-time low of three percent.
"But this does not exclude the possibility of temporary phases of correction on the capital market -- as happened in the previous year."

Zeitler also said it remained to be seen whether the March slowdown in M3 money supply growth to an annualised rate of 8.3 percent from 9.1 percent signalled a "trend change" towards the target range of 3.5 percent to 6.5 percent.

He noted that the M3 figures had to be viewed against the background of a weakening of monetary capital formation and of the growth of extended M3 -- a measure which comprises money market funds and foreign deposits and which has expanded more slowly than M3 by 2.5 percentage points in 1996.
"With this necessary analysis and supplementation the M3 figures for the year 1996 lose drama. But they remain a factor."

Zeitler also said Germany had good prospects to reach economic growth of about 2.5 percent in 1997 as bond yields were below their long-term average and the exchange rate position was benefiting German exporters.

He said structural improvements were needed to fight German unemployment and urged greater labour market flexibility and a reform of the pension system. "The monetary conditions for growth and employment are given," Zeitler said.
